lesson.title: Stitching Points Into a Path: Continuity on an Interval
lesson.summary: A function is continuous on an interval when it passes the pointwise continuity test at every single location inside that interval, with one-sided checks at closed endpoints. This turns the local idea of continuity at a point into a property of an entire stretch of the domain.
lesson.body:
Continuity at a single point c requires three conditions to line up at once: f(c) must be defined, the limit lim(x to c) f(x) must exist, and that limit must equal f(c). Continuity on an interval simply repeats this three part test at every point inside the interval, not just one. Picture checking an entire fence line for gaps rather than inspecting a single post. If even one point along the interval fails the test, whether because the function is undefined there, jumps, or blows up, the function is not continuous on that interval, no matter how well it behaves everywhere else.

For an open interval (a, b), the check is uniform: every point c in (a, b) is an interior point, so you compare the two-sided limit lim(x to c) f(x) with f(c) at each one. Closed and half-open intervals need a small adjustment at the boundary. At the left endpoint a, there are no domain points to the left of a within the interval, so a two-sided limit does not make sense there. Instead the definition requires the right-hand limit to match: lim(x to a+) f(x) = f(a). Symmetrically, at a right endpoint b the definition requires lim(x to b-) f(x) = f(b). This endpoint rule is exactly what the next concept, one-sided continuity, names and formalizes.

Worked example: let f(x) = sqrt(x), and claim it is continuous on [0, infinity). Pick any interior point c > 0. By the limit law for roots, which is valid because c > 0 keeps us safely inside the domain, lim(x to c) sqrt(x) = sqrt(c) = f(c), so the two-sided test passes at every c > 0. At the left endpoint x = 0 there is no two-sided limit to check, since sqrt(x) is undefined for x < 0, so instead we check the right-hand limit: lim(x to 0+) sqrt(x) = 0, and f(0) = 0, so that one-sided condition holds too. Every point of [0, infinity) passes its test, so f is continuous on the whole interval.

Now contrast that with g(x) = 1/x on the interval [-1, 1]. This function is continuous at every point of [-1, 1] except x = 0, where it is not even defined. Because continuity on an interval demands success at every point, and x = 0 sits inside [-1, 1], g fails to be continuous on that interval, even though g is perfectly continuous on the two pieces (-1, 0) and (0, 1) taken separately. This is a common trap: a function can be continuous at almost every point of an interval and still not qualify as continuous on that interval, because almost is not the same as all.

Why insist on continuity across a whole interval rather than at isolated points? Because the major theorems of calculus are stated for intervals. The Intermediate Value Theorem promises that a function continuous on [a, b] hits every value between f(a) and f(b). The Extreme Value Theorem promises that such a function attains an actual maximum and minimum somewhere on [a, b]. Both guarantees collapse if even one point inside the interval is broken, which is exactly why mathematicians insist on the stronger, interval-wide version of continuity rather than settling for continuity at scattered points.
